issues.legal_issue: A presumption of culpability based on possession of contraband cannot arise unless the prosecution first proves conscious possession beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The contraband was recovered from a locked house that the appellant did not live in.
The appellant and a village witness identified the house as belonging to the co-accused, and the village records were said to corroborate that identification.
The appellant promptly gave the police a sale agreement showing a transfer of the house to the co-accused, but the police did not investigate its genuineness or verify the village records.
The prosecution did not examine the village witness to the sale agreement, and the evidence did not establish that the appellant used the house as a storeroom.
The conviction rested substantially on an older voters-list entry recording the appellant as owner.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution did not establish the appellant’s conscious possession beyond reasonable doubt, so the statutory presumptions could not be applied and the conviction was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 35(2) and 54 of the NDPS Act, the presumptions concerning culpability and possession are rebuttable and arise only after the prosecution proves the foundational fact of possession beyond reasonable doubt. The accused’s burden is on a preponderance of probabilities, but that does not lower the prosecution’s burden. Noor Aga v. State of Punjab, (2008) 16 SCC 417, explains that possession must be proved beyond reasonable doubt before the burden shifts; the stringent sentencing provisions call for heightened scrutiny of the foundational facts. The Court also referred to Gopal v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2002) 9 SCC 595.

rule.if: controlled_substance_prosecution and contraband_recovered_from_property and (property_control_uncertain or evidence_does_not_show_conscious_possession) and material_possession_evidence_not_properly_investigated

predicates.controlled_substance_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution alleging an offence involving controlled substances.
predicates.contraband_recovered_from_property: Authorities recovered contraband from a property alleged to be connected to the accused.
predicates.property_control_uncertain: The evidence leaves uncertain whether the accused owned, controlled, or possessed the property where the contraband was found.
predicates.evidence_does_not_show_conscious_possess: The evidence does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the accused knowingly possessed the contraband.
predicates.material_possession_evidence_not_properl: Investigators failed to examine or verify material evidence bearing on who owned or possessed the property.

issues.definition: When a controlled-substance prosecution concerns contraband found on property whose control is uncertain, the evidence does not establish knowing possession, and material possession evidence was not properly investigated, the possession presumption is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A seriously deficient investigation that leaves material evidence about possession unexamined can deny an accused the right to a fair investigation as part of a fair trial.
material_facts: The police did not investigate a sale agreement submitted by the appellant the day after the recovery.
The police did not verify public village records bearing on ownership and possession, despite acknowledging their relevance.
The prosecution did not examine the village witness who was knowledgeable about the property and had witnessed the sale agreement.
The investigation relied on a voters-list entry and an unsupported assertion that the appellant used the property as a storeroom.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was denied the right to a fair investigation, which is a facet of the fair-trial guarantee under Article 21.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 guarantees an accused a fair trial, of which a fair investigation is a facet. The Court held that a casual, perfunctory investigation that failed to examine readily available material evidence denied that right.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution against an accused person.
predicates.material_evidence_bearing_on_accuseds_in: Material evidence bearing on whether the accused was involved was available to investigators.
predicates.investigators_failed_to_examine_material: Investigators failed to examine or verify that material evidence.
predicates.investigation_grossly_deficient: The investigation was casual or perfunctory in a way that materially impaired examination of the evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, when available material evidence about the accused’s involvement is left unexamined in a grossly deficient investigation, the fair-investigation right is violated.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings when the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, the evidence is wholly insufficient, and the lower courts grossly misappreciated it to the point of perversity, particularly where liberty is at stake.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the appellant, and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
The findings of guilt rested on evidence that did not establish conscious possession and on assumptions unsupported by the record.
The investigation left important evidence unexamined, and the evidence as a whole was insufficient to establish the prosecution’s case beyond reasonable doubt.
The appellant had suffered incarceration under the conviction.
issues.conclusion: The Court was not inhibited from reviewing the concurrent findings; it set aside the conviction, acquitted the appellant, and directed his release unless required in another case.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Court normally does not use Article 136 of the Constitution to reappreciate evidence or interfere with concurrent factual findings, it may intervene to protect individual liberty where the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, the evidence is wholly insufficient, and the lower courts’ gross misappreciation of evidence borders on perversity.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_under_special_leave and concurrent_conviction_findings and prosecution_failed_to_establish_prima_facie_case and evidence_wholly_insufficient and lower_courts_grossly_misappreciated_evidence and liberty_at_stake

predicates.criminal_appeal_under_special_leave: The proceeding is a criminal appeal seeking special-leave review of a conviction.
predicates.concurrent_conviction_findings: The trial court convicted the accused and an appellate court affirmed the conviction.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_establish_prima_fa: The prosecution did not establish a prima facie case against the accused.
predicates.evidence_wholly_insufficient: The evidence was wholly insufficient to support the conviction.
predicates.lower_courts_grossly_misappreciated_evid: The lower courts grossly misappreciated the evidence, with their conclusions bordering on perversity.
predicates.liberty_at_stake: The challenged findings place the accused’s liberty at stake.

issues.definition: When a criminal special-leave appeal challenges concurrent convictions and the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, the evidence is wholly insufficient, the lower courts grossly misappreciated it, and liberty is at stake, the Supreme Court may interfere.
